## Definition

Input $n\ge1$, a nonempty family of Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices enclosed by complex rectangles, a point matrix $V\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a real diagonal matrix $\Theta\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, and proposed nonnegative bounds $\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau$. Treat point data as exact dyadics and the family as any subset of its enclosure.

1. With outward interval evaluation, enclose $V^*V-I$ and every $AV-V\Theta$ for the full family. Form Frobenius upper bounds $d,r$ for these two matrices. Also form Frobenius upper bounds $m_A$ for every $A$ in the family and $m_\Theta$ for $\Theta$. If any enclosure or square-root operation is non-finite, return `inconclusive`.

2. Verify by outward scalar comparisons that $d\le\delta<1$, $r\le\rho$, $m_A\le M_A$, $m_\Theta\le M_\Theta$, and that $1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\tau$. If any comparison is undecided or false, return `inconclusive` with the failed check. Otherwise set $\eta=\rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau$ by outward arithmetic and return `certified` with the intervals $[\theta_{(k)}-\eta,\theta_{(k)}+\eta]$, sorted increasingly by the diagonal entries of $\Theta$.

The checks use the Frobenius norm as an upper bound for the operator 2-norm. An inconclusive check makes no statement about the true spectrum.

## Definition

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $v\ne0$, and choose integers
$1\le r<m\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a restart budget
$N_{\max}\ge1$, a target rule, and a restart mode `thick` or `implicit`.
All operations below are in exact arithmetic. In thick mode, the target rule
selects $r-k$ linearly independent current Ritz vectors, where $k$ denotes
the number of already locked pairs; if it cannot do so, the procedure returns
`rank-loss`. In implicit
mode, a shift rule supplies exactly $p=m-r$ complex shifts for the current
cycle, or reports that the shift list is unavailable. The shifts may be chosen
from unwanted Ritz values, but the procedure allows any supplied list and
asserts no convergence for an arbitrary schedule. Initialize the restart
counter $c=0$ before the first Arnoldi cycle. A cycle consists of expanding
the current Arnoldi basis to dimension $m$ or exact breakdown, then computing
Ritz pairs and testing their original residuals. After the initial cycle in
step 1, each restart in step 3 or 4 constructs the next cycle. The output is
the locked Ritz pairs, the current unlocked Ritz pairs, and one of `converged`,
`budget-exhausted`, `invariant-subspace-breakdown`, `rank-loss`,
`shift-count-unavailable`, or `filtered-breakdown`.

1. Start with $v_1=v/\|v\|_2$, no locked pairs, and run fully reorthogonalized
   Arnoldi to dimension $m$, stopping earlier if the next Arnoldi residual is
   zero. Normalize every nonzero projected eigenvector $y$ so $\|y\|_2=1$ and
   lift it to $u=V_my$. For each Ritz pair $(\theta,u)$, compute the original
   residual $r_u=Au-\theta u$ (on a standard Arnoldi cycle it may be evaluated
   by [[prop-ritz-residual-formula-for-an-arnoldi-ritz-pair]]) and accept the
   pair when $\|r_u\|_2\le\tau$. Accepted pairs are recorded as locked outputs
   and their vectors must be retained at every later restart. If at least $r$
   pairs have been accepted, return `converged`.

2. If the projected Arnoldi space is exactly invariant and fewer than $r$ pairs
   have been accepted, return `invariant-subspace-breakdown`. If the restart
   counter satisfies $c=N_{\max}$, return `budget-exhausted`.

3. For a thick restart, form a target block from every locked vector and the
   additional wanted Ritz vectors selected by the target rule. Apply exact
   exact column-pivoted QR as in
   [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]] to
   this block; if its rank is too small to retain all
   locked and selected directions, return `rank-loss`. With the resulting
   orthonormal basis $U$, compute the residual block
   $R_U=(I-UU^*)AU$. Apply exact column-pivoted QR as in
   [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]] to
   $R_U$, breaking pivot
   ties by original column order, to obtain an ordered orthonormal basis $F$ of
   its range. If $U$ has $q$ columns, retain only the first
   $\min(\dim\operatorname{range}(R_U),m-q)$ columns of $F$, so $[U,F]$ has at
   most $m$ columns. Restart from $[U,F]$ and extend by block Arnoldi, fully
   reorthogonalizing each new $Aq$ against all current columns, until the basis
   has dimension $m$ or the exact residual vanishes. If the retained subspace
   is invariant before dimension $m$ and fewer than $r$ pairs are accepted,
   return `invariant-subspace-breakdown`.

4. For an implicit restart, use this branch only when no pair is locked. Set
   $p=m-r$ and request a shift list $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_p$ from the shift rule;
   if it reports a list of the wrong length, return `shift-count-unavailable`.
   Starting from $AV_m=V_mH_m+\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*$, apply exact shifted QR
   steps to $H_m$ using the Givens transformations of
   [[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] in top-down adjacent-row
   eliminations on pairs
   $(1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)$:
   $H_{j-1}-\mu_jI=Q_jR_j$ and $H_j=Q_j^*H_{j-1}Q_j=R_jQ_j+\mu_jI$.
   Put $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_p$, rotate $V_m$ by $Q$, retain its first $r$ columns,
   and continue Arnoldi to dimension $m$. If the polynomial
   $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^p(z-\mu_j)$ annihilates the starting vector or the
   filtered Krylov space has dimension below $r$, return `filtered-breakdown`.

5. Increment the restart counter by setting $c\gets c+1$, recompute Ritz
   pairs and their original residuals, apply the acceptance rule in step 1,
   and return to step 2 unless a return status applies.
   No convergence is asserted for an arbitrary shift schedule. The residual
   acceptance test certifies only the computed residual size; it does not by
   itself give a forward eigenvalue bound for a nonnormal matrix.

## Definition

Input $n\ge1$, nonempty families $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $\mathcal b\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, each enclosed entrywise by finite complex rectangles, together with stored point proposals $R$ and $\widehat x$. The represented family need only be a subset of the supplied product of rectangles; correlations between entries may be discarded. All stored point data are exact dyadics.

1. Use outward rectangle operations to evaluate the expression DAGs
$$
E(A)=I-RA,\qquad c(A,b)=R(b-A\widehat x)
$$
over the full input rectangles. If an operation has no finite enclosure or returns a domain or range status, return `inconclusive`.

2. For each complex rectangle entry $X+iY$, outward-enclose its modulus by computing $\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ and taking the upper endpoint. Combine those bounds by outward sums of squares and square roots to obtain $q\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|E(A)\|_F$ and $r\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,b\in\mathcal b}\|c(A,b)\|_2$. If any modulus, sum, square root or final division has no finite outward result, return `inconclusive`. The Frobenius upper bound also bounds the operator 2-norm. If $q\ge1$, return `inconclusive` with $q,r$. Otherwise return `certified` with the uniform residual data $(R,\widehat x,q,r)$ and radius $r/(1-q)$, rounded outward if represented as a ball.

The interval DAG encloses every value for every admitted pair, including dependencies between repeated inputs because natural interval evaluation may enlarge the range. `inconclusive` makes no assertion that a member is singular.

## Definition

An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. At finite overflow, a directed result is
the corresponding infinite sentinel and its error bound is $+\infty$; the
status is `overflow`. The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of $\mathbb F$.

## Definition

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

## Definition

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

## Definition

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$

$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

## Definition

Input $n\ge1$, a nonempty family of Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices enclosed by complex rectangles, a point matrix $V\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a real diagonal matrix $\Theta\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, and proposed nonnegative bounds $\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau$. Treat point data as exact dyadics and the family as any subset of its enclosure.

1. With outward interval evaluation, enclose $V^*V-I$ and every $AV-V\Theta$ for the full family. Form Frobenius upper bounds $d,r$ for these two matrices. Also form Frobenius upper bounds $m_A$ for every $A$ in the family and $m_\Theta$ for $\Theta$. If any enclosure or square-root operation is non-finite, return `inconclusive`.

2. Verify by outward scalar comparisons that $d\le\delta<1$, $r\le\rho$, $m_A\le M_A$, $m_\Theta\le M_\Theta$, and that $1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\tau$. If any comparison is undecided or false, return `inconclusive` with the failed check. Otherwise set $\eta=\rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau$ by outward arithmetic and return `certified` with the intervals $[\theta_{(k)}-\eta,\theta_{(k)}+\eta]$, sorted increasingly by the diagonal entries of $\Theta$.

The checks use the Frobenius norm as an upper bound for the operator 2-norm. An inconclusive check makes no statement about the true spectrum.
